title: Chapter 8.  History — 1947: Partition, Instrument of Accession & the First Kashmir War

blocks.content: The events of 1947 are the single most consequential chapter in J&K's modern political history — the princely state's ambiguous position at Partition, the tribal invasion, Maharaja Hari Singh's accession to India, and the resulting first India-Pakistan war together explain nearly every subsequent political and constitutional development covered in this book.
The Princely States & the Choice at Partition

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Princely States were required to choose accession between India and Pakistan during Partition in 1947.
The tribal invasion into Jammu & Kashmir necessitated external military assistance.
Maharaja Hari Singh signed the Instrument of Accession to formally accede to the Union of India.
The First Kashmir War (1947-48) concluded with the intervention of the United Nations.

blocks.content: Under the Indian Independence Act, 1947, British paramountcy over India's roughly 560 princely states lapsed, and each state's ruler was left free to accede to either India or Pakistan (or, in principle, remain independent), guided by considerations of geographic contiguity and the wishes of the population, though the Act itself did not mandate a plebiscite.

Maharaja Hari Singh of Jammu and Kashmir initially sought to delay this choice, exploring the possibility of remaining independent (or negotiating a standstill agreement with both India and Pakistan to maintain existing administrative arrangements), given the state's mixed population — a Muslim-majority Kashmir Valley alongside Hindu-majority Jammu areas and Buddhist-majority Ladakh — and its position straddling both prospective dominions.
Pakistan signed a standstill agreement with the state in August 1947, while India did not, pending further negotiation.
The Tribal Invasion & Accession to India
1947: Partition, Instrument of Accession & the First Kashmir War

In October 1947, Pashtun tribal militias (widely understood to have been armed and facilitated with support from Pakistan) invaded the state from the west, advancing rapidly toward Srinagar via Muzaffarabad and Baramulla, precipitating a crisis for the Maharaja's administration.

Facing this invasion and lacking the military capacity to repel it alone, Maharaja Hari Singh appealed to India for military assistance; the Government of India, through Governor-General Lord Mountbatten, made clear that assistance could only be provided once the state formally acceded to India.

Maharaja Hari Singh signed the Instrument of Accession on 26 October 1947, formally acceding Jammu and Kashmir to the Dominion of India on the same terms as other acceding princely states — ceding to the Indian Parliament legislative authority over Defence, External Affairs and Communications, while retaining autonomy over all other subjects. Indian troops were airlifted into Srinagar beginning 27 October 1947, halting the tribal advance short of the city.

India's acceptance of the accession, communicated by Lord Mountbatten, included an accompanying statement that once law and order were restored, the question of accession would be settled by a reference to the people (a plebiscite) — a commitment frequently cited in later political and diplomatic debate, though never carried out, and whose exact legal status and binding character remain a matter of continuing dispute between India and Pakistan.

cells: Indian Independence Act comes into force; British paramountcy lapses
Pakistan-J&K standstill agreement signed (India does not sign one)
Instrument of Accession signed by Maharaja Hari Singh

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: The Instrument of Accession (26 October 1947) is arguably the single most important date in this entire book — it is the legal foundation for Jammu and Kashmir's status as part of India, and the starting point for both Article 370 (Chapter 9) and the wider India-Pakistan dispute over the region.
The First Kashmir War (1947-48) & UN Involvement

Following the accession, fighting between Indian forces (supported by state forces and local volunteer militias including the pro-accession National Conference's own cadres) and the Pakistan-backed tribal/irregular forces (later joined by regular Pakistani troops) continued through 1947-48, in what is termed India's First Kashmir War (or the First India-Pakistan War).

India referred the dispute to the newly formed United Nations in January 1948, leading to UN Security Council Resolutions calling for a ceasefire and, eventually, a plebiscite to determine the region's future status, contingent on the withdrawal of Pakistani forces and tribal militias from the territory they had occupied — a precondition that was never fulfilled, and the plebiscite consequently never took place.

items: The Instrument of Accession was executed by Maharaja Hari Singh in October 1947 to integrate Jammu & Kashmir into India.
The First Kashmir War led directly to United Nations mediation and the establishment of a Ceasefire Line.

blocks.content: A ceasefire came into effect on 1 January 1949, establishing the Ceasefire Line — later renamed the Line of Control (LoC) after the Simla Agreement of 1972 — which divided the former princely state into Indian-administered Jammu and Kashmir (including Ladakh) and Pakistan-administered territory (subsequently organised by Pakistan as 'Azad Jammu and Kashmir' and the separately administered 'Northern Areas', now called Gilgit-Baltistan).

★ EXAM POINT: The Ceasefire Line of 1 January 1949 was RENAMED the Line of Control (LoC) only after the 1972 Simla Agreement — these are the same physical boundary under two different names at two different points in history, a frequently tested nomenclature-and-date question.

items: Instrument of Accession signed by Maharaja Hari Singh: 26 October 1947, acceding J&K to India (Defence, External Affairs, Communications ceded to India).
Indian troops airlifted into Srinagar from 27 October 1947, halting the Pakistan-backed tribal invasion.
India referred the dispute to the UN in January 1948; UN resolutions called for a plebiscite contingent on Pakistani withdrawal, which never occurred.
Ceasefire came into effect 1 January 1949, creating the Ceasefire Line — renamed the Line of Control (LoC) after the 1972 Simla Agreement.
This 1947-49 sequence is the direct origin of both Article 370 (Chapter 9) and the continuing India-Pakistan territorial dispute over the region.
